title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
This incident is an impersonation scam in which AI-generated content was used to fabricate a fake interview between two named public figures, Alan Kohler and Michele Bullock, in order to promote an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform called Boulder Sparhaven. The failure happened at the content-production and distribution stage, entirely outside any legitimate deployment: scammers used AI tools to generate convincing text and, reportedly, deepfakes, then circulated the output as if it were real journalism. Catching it would have required either platform-level detection of synthetically generated content before distribution, or a reader checking the claimed source against the actual ABC archive.

The pattern ASIC describes is not a malfunction of a deployed product but a deliberate misuse of AI generation capabilities to scale fraud. The volume figures, 19,400 scams removed in a single year at a 182 percent increase, indicate that the tooling lowers the cost of producing individually convincing material to the point where mass production becomes practical. The specific mechanism, a fake confrontational interview designed to seem newsworthy, is a form of false-context framing in which synthetic content is given the appearance of editorial credibility.

What is not established is whether any specific AI platform or company was responsible for producing the fake material, how many people were harmed by this particular article, or whether Boulder Sparhaven's operators have been identified or charged.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
A fabricated article featuring a fake interview between ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler and Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock exemplifies a rising wave of investment scams. The article falsely claimed Bullock became angry during questioning about Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform. The interview never occurred, yet this type of deception is becoming increasingly common as scammers use artificial intelligence to create convincing deepfakes and fake content involving prominent Australians.

Australian Securities and Investments Commission research reveals investment scams are growing more sophisticated and prevalent. Last year, ASIC removed 19,400 scams, a 182 percent increase, including 7,051 fake investment platforms and 5,476 phishing scams. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, financial commentator Alan Kohler, and billionaire Gina Rinehart are among the most frequently impersonated public figures. ASIC urges consumers to verify Australian Financial Services licence numbers through its free public register before investing and warns that polished content and familiar branding do not guarantee legitimacy.
